front: According to Rosenblum & Garfinkel, when and as what did the VMM originally come into being?
back: At the end of the 1960s, as a software-abstraction layer that partitions a hardware platform into one or more VMs, each similar enough to the physical machine to run existing software unmodified.

front: What problem drove the 1990s Stanford revival of VMs, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Massively parallel processing (MPP) machines that were hard to program and could not run existing operating systems. Researchers used VMs to make these machines look similar enough to existing platforms to reuse current operating systems.

front: What did the Stanford MPP virtualization project produce, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: The people and ideas behind VMware.

front: Why did admins resort to one-application-per-machine, and how does that connect to the VMM's return, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: One-application-per-machine limited crashes and break-ins but raised hardware requirements; consolidating those into VMs on a few platforms is what returned the VMM to prominence under the banner of server consolidation and utility computing.

front: How do Rosenblum & Garfinkel describe the benefit VMMs give OS developers for deploying innovation?
back: A backward-compatible path to deploy innovation that is no longer practical inside "complex and ossified" operating systems where "innovation moves at a geologic pace."

front: What is the "classic VMM" in Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: A thin layer exporting a VM abstraction that looks enough like the hardware that any software for that hardware runs in the VM.

front: What does Rosenblum & Garfinkel's "uniform view of hardware" provided by the VMM enable?
back: It makes machines with different I/O subsystems look the same, so a VM can run on any available computer.

front: What encapsulation consequences does Rosenblum & Garfinkel enumerate for mapping and migrating VMs?
back: The VMM can map and remap VMs to hardware at will and migrate them; load balancing and hardware-failure handling become a remap; and VMs are easy to replicate.

front: What general-purpose capability does the VMM's ability to suspend, resume, checkpoint, and roll back VMs give, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: A general-purpose undo for recovering from crashes or misconfiguration.

front: What general mobility model does encapsulation support, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Copying a suspended VM over a network or on removable media.

front: What gives strong isolation in a VMM, and to what two properties does Rosenblum & Garfinkel tie it?
back: Total mediation of VM-hardware interaction gives strong isolation, tied to reliability (a crashing app's OS fault stays contained) and security (a compromised app's attacker is contained to one VM).

text: Rosenblum & Garfinkel name three central VMM design goals: {{c1::compatibility}} (run legacy software), {{c2::performance}} (run at close to native speed), and {{c3::simplicity}}.
extra: This implementation-facing triad differs from the lecture's Popek-Goldberg fidelity, performance, and safety and isolation, which comes from a different paper.

front: Why does Rosenblum & Garfinkel's simplicity design goal matter?
back: A VMM failure takes down all its VMs, and secure isolation needs a bug-free VMM.

front: How do Rosenblum & Garfinkel define a virtualizable CPU architecture?
back: One that supports direct execution: running the VM on the real machine while the VMM keeps ultimate control of the CPU.

front: In Rosenblum & Garfinkel's disable-interrupts example, how does the VMM safely handle a guest trying to disable interrupts?
back: Letting the guest disable interrupts would be unsafe (the VMM could not regain control), so the VMM traps it, records that interrupts are disabled for that VM, and postpones delivering interrupts until the VM re-enables them.

front: What goal do Rosenblum & Garfinkel state precisely for CPU virtualization trap semantics?
back: Provide trap semantics letting the VMM safely, transparently, and directly use the CPU to run the VM.

front: Why did academic projects favor paravirtualization but commodity products did not, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Building a VMM with both full compatibility and high performance is a significant engineering challenge, so academic projects accepted paravirtualization despite its incompatibility; VMware, aiming at fast, compatible x86 virtualization (huge amounts of legacy x86 software make giving up compatibility nontrivial), built direct execution plus binary translation instead.

front: What is memory overcommit, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Like an OS's virtual memory, the VMM can page a VM to disk, letting memory allocated to VMs exceed physical memory, so the workload needs less hardware; the VMM dynamically controls each VM's memory.

front: Why is it a challenge for the VMM to reclaim memory by paging VMs out, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: The guest OS has better page-replacement knowledge; for example, it knows a page's creating process exited.

front: How does the VMware ESX Server balloon process reclaim guest memory, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: To reclaim memory the VMM "inflates" the balloon, the guest picks pages to give it using its own replacement policy, and the balloon hands them to the VMM. It is a paravirtualization-like process inside the guest.

front: Why is software shadowing of page tables costly, and what future direction do Rosenblum & Garfinkel flag?
back: Operating systems change page tables frequently, so software shadowing is costly; hardware-managed shadow page tables (long present in mainframe virtualization) are a fruitful direction.

front: Beyond hardware-managed shadow page tables, what two open research areas does Rosenblum & Garfinkel flag for memory?
back: Cooperative VMM/guest resource management and data-center-level resource management.

front: How does VMware ESX Server's architecture differ from the hosted architecture, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: It runs directly on hardware without a host OS, with sophisticated scheduling and resource management and a highly optimized I/O subsystem; it borrows Linux kernel device drivers to talk directly to devices.

front: What shift in I/O devices eases virtualization, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel's future outlook?
back: Discrete I/O devices (the original IBM PC keyboard and IDE controllers) are giving way to channel-like devices (USB, SCSI); with hardware support, channel I/O devices could be passed directly to the VM with no VMM trap.

front: What three requirements does Rosenblum & Garfinkel list for passing channel I/O devices directly to a VM?
back:
• Devices must know about VMs and support multiple virtual interfaces.
  • DMA-capable devices need address remapping so a VM driver accesses only its VM's memory.
  • The VMM needs efficient routing of device-completion interrupts to the correct VM.

front: What server-side management future does Rosenblum & Garfinkel envision for VMs?
back: Admins provisioning, monitoring, and managing thousands of VMs on hundreds of boxes from one console, instantiating servers from templates and treating computers as a generic resource pool.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What does hot migration (VMware VMotion) make possible on the server side, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: A highly dynamic VM-to-hardware mapping: hardware failure is handled by remapping VMs, and maintenance, lease ends, and upgrades happen without service interruption.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What automated server-management future do Rosenblum & Garfinkel predict, and what product is their example?
back: Automated load balancing, failure prediction, and demand-driven VM creation and destruction; VMware Virtual Center is the example.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: How do Rosenblum & Garfinkel argue VMs help desktop management "beyond the machine room"?
back: Solving a problem at the VMM layer benefits all software regardless of age or vendor and removes the need for n versions of help-desk/backup software; VMs also change user mental models (easy create/copy/share).
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What mobility examples and infrastructure needs does Rosenblum & Garfinkel cite for the desktop?
back: Increased mobility (The Collective, Internet Suspend/Resume) lets a user's whole computing environment migrate over LAN/WAN or ride on a USB drive; dynamic environments need virtual switches, virtual firewalls, and overlay networks.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: How does moving host-based security outside the VM improve it, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Running it alongside but isolated from the OS gives the same function with much stronger attack resistance.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What two VMM-based security research examples does Rosenblum & Garfinkel name, and what does each do?
back: Livewire (VMM-based intrusion detection) and ReVirt (VMM logging/replay to analyze a break-in).
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What high-assurance isolation example using VMware does Rosenblum & Garfinkel cite?
back: NSA NetTop, which uses VMware to isolate networks of different classifications.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: Besides high-assurance systems, what two other isolation-based security uses of VMMs does Rosenblum & Garfinkel name?
back: Network quarantine, and running multiple software stacks at different security levels.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: How are VMs a building block for trusted computing, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Via remote attestation (Terra), illustrated by a desktop running low-security Web-browsing, hardened-Linux day-to-day, and high-security mail VMs that servers can attest before granting access.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What does Rosenblum & Garfinkel say flexible resource management helps resist?
back: Flash crowds and DDoS.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What software-distribution model do VMMs enable, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Vendors can ship entire preconfigured VMs; the model can serve production, not just demos.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What distribution example does Rosenblum & Garfinkel give for shipping VMs?
back: Oracle distributed 10,000+ copies of its database environment as VMs.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What are virtual appliances, and what tool controls VM publishing, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: The Collective explored bundling applications as virtual appliances whose maintainer handles patching; VMware ACE lets admins publish and control VMs.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: How will the VM distribution model force software licensing to change, per Rosenblum & Garfinkel?
back: Licensing will shift from per-CPU/per-machine toward use-based or sitewide licenses.
source: What's ahead (server side, beyond the machine room, security, software distribution)

front: What is Rosenblum & Garfinkel's conclusion about the VMM resurgence?
back: The VMM resurgence is fundamentally altering how designers view, manage, and structure complex software environments, and provides a backward-compatible path for innovative OS solutions.
